title: Comparing things and people
objectives: I can compare two things or people with 'mais', 'menos', 'tão' and 'tanto', and explain why the second thing is introduced by 'que', 'do que', 'quanto' or 'de'.
I can use the irregular comparatives 'melhor', 'pior', 'maior' and 'menor', and explain why they never take 'mais'.
I can say that something is the best, the most or the least in a group, and intensify an adjective with '-íssimo', including the spelling and accent changes it causes.
I can say that things are the same, similar or different, state a preference, and give an opinion about places and products.
I can explain why the accents and unusual letters in this unit's words are written as they are, and I can tell a literal word-for-word meaning from a natural translation.

vocabulary.note: 'Caro' means 'dear' in both senses, costly and beloved, exactly as English 'dear' does; that is why a letter opens 'Caro Pedro', Dear Pedro. Feminine 'cara', plural 'caros'. A single 'r' between vowels is a quick tap [ɾ], and the double 'rr' of 'carro' (car) is the strong sound, so 'caro' and 'carro' are different words.

example.target: Esse tênis é mais caro do que o outro.
example.source: This sneaker is more expensive than the other one.
example.source_literal: This sneaker is more dear of-the that the other.

vocabulary.note: Usually just means low-priced, with less of a negative edge than English 'cheap'. The saying 'O barato sai caro', literally 'the cheap leaves dear', means cheap things cost you more in the end. Stress is the default for an ending in 'o', the second to last syllable: ba-RA-to.

example.target: O ônibus é mais barato do que o táxi.
example.source: The bus is cheaper than the taxi.
example.source_literal: The bus is more cheap of-the that the taxi.

vocabulary.note: RÁ-pi-do is stressed on the third to last syllable, which no ending predicts, so the accent is always written; it is acute because the 'á' is open. The accent disappears in 'rapidíssimo' (see the note on '-íssimo').

example.target: O avião é muito mais rápido do que o ônibus.
example.source: The plane is much faster than the bus.
example.source_literal: The plane is very more fast of-the that the bus.

vocabulary.note: Says both 'tall' (people) and 'high' (prices, sounds). The 'l' closes the syllable, so it is said like 'w': [ˈawtu]. The opposite for height is 'baixo', low or short ('mais baixo'). The 'x' of 'baixo' is said [ʃ], like the 'sh' of 'shoe', because an 'x' between a diphthong and a vowel is [ʃ].

example.target: Meu irmão é mais alto do que eu.
example.source: My brother is taller than I am.
example.source_literal: My brother is more tall of-the that I.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the second to last syllable (con-for-TÁ-vel), but an ending in 'l' defaults to the last syllable, so the accent is required. The plural is 'confortáveis': the final 'l' becomes 'i', and the accent stays because the stress has not moved. One form for masculine and feminine.

example.target: Este sofá é tão confortável quanto a minha cama.
example.source: This sofa is as comfortable as my bed.
example.source_literal: This sofa is so comfortable as-much-as the my bed.

vocabulary.note: From 'divertir', to amuse. In most of Brazil the 'd' and the 't' before an 'i' are said [dʒ] and [tʃ], like the 'j' of 'jam' and the 'ch' of 'cheese': di-ver-TI-do. Stress is the default for an ending in 'o'.

example.target: O carnaval de rua é muito divertido.
example.source: Street carnival is a lot of fun.
example.source_literal: The carnival of street is very amusing.

vocabulary.note: A 'g' before 'u' is hard anyway, so the 'u' is a real vowel: se-GU-ro. As a noun, 'o seguro' is insurance.

example.target: Este bairro é mais seguro do que o meu.
example.source: This neighborhood is safer than mine.
example.source_literal: This neighborhood is more safe of-the that the mine.

vocabulary.note: Normally the 'u' of 'qu' before 'i' is silent, but 'tranquilo' is one of the handful of words where it is pronounced: tran-KWI-lo. The 'an' is a nasal vowel.

example.target: O interior é mais tranquilo do que a capital.
example.source: The countryside is calmer than the capital.
example.source_literal: The interior is more calm of-the that the capital.

vocabulary.note: Ends in 'l', said like 'w', and an ending in 'l' is stressed on the last syllable by default: ca-pi-TAL, no accent. Feminine when it is the city; 'o capital' is money. In São Paulo state, 'a capital' often means the city of São Paulo itself.

example.target: Brasília é a capital do Brasil.
example.source: Brasília is the capital of Brazil.

vocabulary.note: Means the inland towns away from the capital or the coast, not only the inside of a building. Ends in 'r', so stress falls on the last syllable without an accent: in-te-ri-OR.

example.target: Minha avó mora no interior de Minas.
example.source: My grandmother lives in the countryside of Minas.
example.source_literal: My grandmother lives in-the interior of Minas.

vocabulary.note: Li-to-RAL: ends in 'l', so stressed on the last syllable, no accent, and the 'l' is said like 'w'. Related to the English word 'littoral'.

example.target: O litoral do Nordeste tem praias lindas.
example.source: The coast of the Northeast has beautiful beaches.
example.source_literal: The coast of-the Northeast has beaches beautiful.

vocabulary.note: From 'marcar', to mark. The 'r' closes the first syllable (MAR-ca), and the sound of a syllable-final 'r' depends on the region: a strong 'h'-like sound in much of Brazil, a tap or a trill elsewhere. The stress is the default for an ending in 'a'.

example.target: Qual é a melhor marca de celular?
example.source: What is the best phone brand?
example.source_literal: Which is the better brand of cellphone?

vocabulary.note: 'Qu' before 'a': the 'u' is pronounced [w], as in 'quando': kwa-li-DA-de. The final 'de' is said [dʒi], because 'd' before 'i' or a weak final 'e' is [dʒ].

example.target: A qualidade dessa marca é ótima.
example.source: The quality of that brand is great.
example.source_literal: The quality of-this brand is excellent.

vocabulary.note: The cedilla 'ç' writes the sound [s] before 'o', where a plain 'c' would be [k]. A 'ç' is never needed before 'e' or 'i', because 'c' is already [s] there.

example.target: O preço é igual nas duas lojas.
example.source: The price is the same in both stores.
example.source_literal: The price is equal in-the two stores.

vocabulary.note: 'Na minha opinião' is the standard way to introduce your view; Portuguese keeps the article before 'minha' where English has none. The ending 'ão' is nasal and stressed by default: o-pi-ni-ÃO; the plural is 'opiniões'.

example.target: Na minha opinião, Salvador é mais animada do que Recife.
example.source: In my opinion, Salvador is livelier than Recife.
example.source_literal: In-the my opinion, Salvador is more lively of-the that Recife.

vocabulary.note: The comparative of 'bom' (adjective) and of 'bem' (adverb). With the article it means 'the best': 'o melhor'. One form for masculine and feminine; the plural is 'melhores'. 'Lh' is one sound, [ʎ]; the ending 'r' makes the last syllable stressed, so no accent.

example.target: Esse filme é melhor do que o livro.
example.source: This movie is better than the book.
example.source_literal: This film is better of-the that the book.

vocabulary.note: The comparative of 'ruim', 'mau' and 'mal'. With the article it means 'the worst': 'o pior'. Pi-OR: ends in 'r', stressed on the last syllable, no accent. Plural 'piores'.

example.target: O trânsito hoje está pior do que ontem.
example.source: Traffic today is worse than yesterday.
example.source_literal: The traffic today is worse of-the that yesterday.

vocabulary.note: The comparative of 'grande'. With the article it means 'the biggest': 'o maior'. Ma-i-OR: the 'i' is a quick glide [j] between the 'a' and the 'o', and the ending 'r' makes the last syllable stressed, so no accent. Plural 'maiores'.

example.target: A minha casa é maior do que a sua.
example.source: My house is bigger than yours.
example.source_literal: The my house is bigger of-the that the yours.

vocabulary.note: The comparative of 'pequeno'. With the article it means 'the smallest': 'o menor'. Me-NOR: the stress is on the last syllable because of the 'r'. Plural 'menores'. 'Mais pequeno' is also correct and common.

example.target: Este quarto é menor do que o meu.
example.source: This room is smaller than mine.
example.source_literal: This room is smaller of-the that the mine.

vocabulary.note: With the article it means 'the oldest': 'o mais velho'. Agrees with the noun: 'mais velha', 'mais velhos'. 'Mais' never changes, only the adjective after it. 'Lh' is one sound, [ʎ].

example.target: Meu irmão é três anos mais velho do que eu.
example.source: My brother is three years older than me.
example.source_literal: My brother is three years more old of-the that I.

vocabulary.note: 'Novo' means both 'new' and 'young', so 'mais novo' is 'younger' when said of people and 'newer' when said of things. Agrees with the noun: 'mais nova', 'mais novos'.

example.target: Minha prima é mais nova do que eu.
example.source: My cousin is younger than me.
example.source_literal: My cousin is more new of-the that I.

vocabulary.note: 'Igual a' means 'the same as'; 'a' + 'o' contracts to 'ao', 'a' + 'a' to 'à'. The 'u' of 'gu' before 'a' is pronounced [w] and the final 'l' is said like 'w': i-GUAL. The plural is 'iguais' ('l' becomes 'i').

example.target: Meu celular é igual ao seu.
example.source: My phone is the same as yours.
example.source_literal: My cellphone is equal to-the yours.

vocabulary.note: 'Parecido' is the adjective made from the verb 'parecer', to seem or to look, so 'parecido com' is literally 'seemed with'. It agrees with the first noun: 'parecida', 'parecidos'. The 'c' before 'i' is said [s]. The verb itself is common: 'Ela parece cansada' means 'she seems tired'.

example.target: Esse bairro é parecido com o meu.
example.source: This neighborhood is similar to mine.
example.source_literal: This neighborhood is seemed with the mine.

vocabulary.note: 'De' contracts with the article: 'diferente do', 'da', 'dos', 'das'. The first 'd' is before an 'i', so it is said [dʒ]; the 'en' is a nasal vowel. One form for masculine and feminine; plural 'diferentes'.

example.target: O Rio é muito diferente de São Paulo.
example.source: Rio is very different from São Paulo.
example.source_literal: The Rio is very different of São Paulo.

vocabulary.note: Also means 'roughly': 'mais ou menos dez reais' is about ten reais. 'Mais' has the diphthong 'ai' and 'ou' is the diphthong [ow], each a single syllable.

example.target: Como foi o filme? Mais ou menos.
example.source: How was the movie? So-so.
example.source_literal: How was the film? More or less.

vocabulary.note: 'Pena' is an older word for trouble, sorrow or effort; the idea is that the effort pays off. Only the verb 'valer' changes: 'vale a pena', 'valeu a pena' (it was worth it), 'não vale a pena'. 'Que pena!' means 'what a pity!' Before an infinitive there is no preposition: 'vale a pena esperar'.

example.target: Vale a pena pagar mais por uma marca melhor?
example.source: Is it worth paying more for a better brand?
example.source_literal: Is-worth the pain to-pay more for a brand better?

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: why the words of this unit are written as they are
grammar.explanation:
Nothing in this unit's spelling is a new rule. Every accent and every unusual letter below follows a rule from the first three lessons, and this note shows those rules at work on the new words so that you can read and write them instead of memorizing them. Two questions solve almost every word. First, where is the stress, and does it agree with the default for the word's ending? Words ending in 'a', 'e' or 'o' (with or without 's') and in 'am', 'em' or 'ens' are stressed on the second to last syllable; words ending in 'i', 'u', 'l', 'r', 'z', 'im', 'um', 'ns', 'is', 'us' or the nasal 'ã' and 'ão' are stressed on the last. When the stress breaks the default, a written accent appears on the stressed vowel: acute (´) when the vowel is open, circumflex (^) when it is closed. Second, what do the neighboring letters say about how each letter is pronounced? The next letter decides 'c' and 'g', a vowel followed by 'm' or 'n' at the end of a syllable is nasal, and the pairs 'lh', 'nh', 'ch', 'rr', 'qu' and 'gu' work as units.

The accents in this unit fall into three groups. Stress on the third to last syllable is never predicted by an ending, so it always takes an accent: 'rápido' (RÁ-pi-do), 'ótimo' (Ó-ti-mo), 'péssimo' (PÉS-si-mo), 'câmera' (CÂ-me-ra), 'trânsito' (TRÂN-si-to), 'tímida' (TÍ-mi-da), and 'família' and 'Brasília', where the ending 'ia' counts as two syllables (fa-MÍ-li-a). Stress on the last syllable of a word whose ending defaults to the second to last also takes an accent: 'sofá', 'até', 'está', 'metrô', and one-syllable words such as 'é', 'lá', 'nós' and 'três'. The mark follows the vowel: open 'ó' in 'nós', closed 'ê' in 'três' and 'ô' in 'metrô'. Finally, stress on the second to last syllable of a word whose ending defaults to the last takes an accent too: 'confortável' (con-for-TÁ-vel) ends in 'l', 'tênis' (TÊ-nis) ends in 'is', and 'táxi' (TÁ-xi) ends in 'i'. The circumflex of 'tênis' shows a closed 'e', which is the usual quality of a stressed 'e' directly before the 'n' that starts the next syllable (the same pattern as the 'e' of 'tema' and the 'o' of 'fome'). Words that only look similar need no mark: 'mais', 'dois' and 'reais' end in 'is', so stress on the last syllable is simply the default, and 'melhor', 'pior', 'maior', 'menor' end in 'r', so they are stressed on the last syllable without any accent.

The consonants follow the lesson on sounds. Between vowels, a single 'r' is a quick tap and 'rr' is the strong sound, so 'caro' (expensive) and 'carro' (car) are different words. A 'c' before 'e' or 'i' is [s] ('celular', 'parecido'), and a cedilla writes [s] before 'o', as in 'preço'. A 'g' before 'e' or 'i' is [ʒ], the sound of the 's' in 'measure' ('região', 'dirige'). The pairs 'lh' and 'nh' are single sounds ('melhor', 'velho', 'escolha', 'ganha'). The 'u' after 'q' or 'g' is pronounced [w] before 'a' ('quando', 'qualidade', 'igual') and silent before 'e' or 'i' ('que', 'quem', 'quieta'), except in a handful of words such as 'tranquilo', where it is pronounced. A letter 'l' at the end of a syllable is said like the 'w' of 'now' ('Sul', 'capital', 'hotel', 'igual', 'alto', 'filme', 'Alfa'), and the 'h' of 'hotel' is silent. In most of Brazil 'd' and 't' before 'i', or before a weak final 'e', are said [dʒ] and [tʃ]: 'diferente', 'divertido', 'time', 'qualidade'. A single 's' between vowels is [z] ('perigoso') and 'ss' is [s] ('péssimo', 'caríssimo', 'ingresso'). An 'x' can be [ks], as in 'táxi'. The endings 'ão' and 'ões' are nasal and, in 'ão', stressed ('região', 'opinião', 'tão').

Two accent facts belong to the ending '-íssimo' and are explained in the note on superlatives: the 'í' of '-íssimo' always carries an accent, and an old accent on the base word is dropped ('rápido' becomes 'rapidíssimo'). Use the table as a checklist. When you meet a new accented word, do not ask whether to memorize the accent: count syllables, find the stress and compare it with the default.

rows: rápido, ótimo, péssimo, câmera, trânsito, tímida, família
Stress on the third to last syllable is never the default, so an accent is always written. Acute for an open vowel or for 'i' and 'u', circumflex for a closed vowel.
The ending 'l' defaults to the last syllable, so stress on the second to last needs an accent. In the plural the 'l' becomes 'i' and the accent stays because the stress has not moved.
Each breaks the default of its ending. The mark follows the vowel: closed 'ê' and 'ô', open 'á' in 'táxi' and 'ó' in 'nós'.
Endings in 'a' and 'e' default to the second to last syllable, so stress on the last takes an acute accent on the open vowel.
mais, dois, reais, melhor, pior, maior, menor
mais, re-AIS, me-LHOR, pi-OR, ma-i-OR, me-NOR
Stress on the last syllable is the default for 'is', 'ois' and 'r', so no accent. The 'o' of the four comparatives is open, which the spelling cannot show.
A single 'r' between vowels is a tap; 'rr' is the strong sound. Two different words.
Before 'e' or 'i' the letter 'c' is already [s]. Before 'a', 'o' or 'u' it would be [k], so 'ç' is written to keep [s].

The 'u' after 'q' or 'g' before 'a' is pronounced [w]. In 'seguro' the 'g' is hard before 'u' anyway. 'Tranquilo' is one of the few words where the 'u' of 'qui' is pronounced; in 'que', 'quem' and 'quieta' it is silent.
'G' before 'e' or 'i' is [ʒ]. 'Ão' is nasal and stressed on the last syllable by default; the ending 'em' of 'viagem' is stressed on the second to last, as the default says.
'Lh' is the sound [ʎ] and 'nh' is [ɲ]. Each pair is one sound and is never split between syllables.
Sul, capital, hotel, igual, alto, filme, Alfa
An 'l' that closes a syllable is said like 'w'. The 'h' of 'hotel' is silent. Final 'l' defaults to a stressed last syllable.
Before 'i', or before a weak final 'e', 'd' is said [dʒ] and 't' is said [tʃ]. The 'en' in 'diferente' is a nasal vowel.
perigoso, péssimo, caríssimo, ingresso, táxi, baixo

A single 's' between vowels is [z]; 'ss' between vowels is [s]. The two spellings keep the sounds apart. The letter 'x' has several sounds: [ks] in 'táxi', and [ʃ] in 'baixo', as the lesson on sounds showed.

grammar.title: Comparing: mais, menos, tão and tanto
grammar.explanation:
A comparison says that one thing has more, less or the same amount of a quality as another thing. The terms used here: an adjective is a word that describes a noun ('caro', 'alto'); a comparative is a construction that compares two things; and the two things are compared on a quality. English has two tools for it: an ending added to short adjectives ('tall', 'taller'; 'cheap', 'cheaper') and the word 'more' for long ones ('more expensive'). Portuguese has one tool only, a separate word placed in front of the adjective. There is no comparative ending, so the length of the adjective never matters: 'mais alto', 'mais barato', 'mais confortável'. 'Mais' (more) and 'menos' (less) build comparisons of inequality, and 'tão' and 'tanto' (as, as much) build comparisons of equality. Four very common adjectives are the exceptions, and the next note explains why.

More and less. The pattern is 'mais' or 'menos', then the adjective, then 'que' or 'do que' for the second thing: 'O carro é mais caro do que a moto'. 'Que' and 'do que' both mean 'than'. 'Que' is shorter and very common in speech; 'do que' is the fuller form, in which 'do' is the preposition 'de' fused with the article 'o' (literally 'of-the that'), and before a plain noun or pronoun you can treat the two as interchangeable. Before a whole clause with its own verb, as in 'mais caro do que eu pensava', use 'do que'. The adjective agrees in gender and number with the first thing, the one being described, and never with the second: 'A moto é menos cara que o carro', with 'cara' because 'moto' is feminine. 'Mais' and 'menos' themselves never change. For an action rather than a quality, 'mais' and 'menos' follow the verb and also stay fixed: 'Ele trabalha mais do que eu'.

Which pronoun comes after 'than'. English says 'than me' in casual speech. Portuguese completes the second half of the comparison as a short sentence with its verb left out: 'Ele é mais alto do que eu' means 'taller than I am', so the word after 'que' is the subject of that understood verb, and the subject form is 'eu'. 'Do que mim' is wrong. 'Mim' is the form that 'I' takes after a preposition ('de mim', 'para mim'), and 'que' is not a preposition.

Leaving out the repeated noun. English avoids repeating a noun with the word 'one' or with a possessive ending: 'the Beta's', 'the one at home'. Portuguese uses the article alone, followed by 'de' and the owner or place: 'a do Beta' means 'the one of the Beta', and 'o de casa' means 'the one at home'. The article still agrees with the noun that is left out, so 'a do Beta' is feminine because it stands for 'a bateria'.

Numbers. Before a number, use 'de' and not 'que': 'Custa mais de cem reais'. 'Que' joins two things that are compared with each other; a number is not a second thing but a limit, and 'de' marks it as the measure of the amount. The same holds for 'menos de'.

Equality. 'Tão' followed by an adjective and then 'quanto' (or 'como') means 'as ... as': 'Ela é tão alta quanto o pai'. 'Tão' is the form of 'tanto' used before an adjective or adverb, and 'quanto' is the question word 'how much' used as a linking word, so the literal reading is 'so tall how-much the father'. With a noun, 'tanto' is an adjective and agrees with it: 'tanto trabalho', 'tanta paciência', 'tantos amigos', 'tantas praias', followed by 'quanto', which stays fixed in everyday speech. With a verb, 'tanto' stays fixed: 'Eu estudo tanto quanto você'. To deny equality, put 'não' in front: 'O Alfa não é tão caro quanto o Beta', not as expensive as the Beta.

grammar.title: Irregular comparatives: melhor, pior, maior, menor
grammar.explanation:
Four very common adjectives have a comparative of their own, and the reason is historical. Latin built comparatives with an ending, and almost every adjective lost that ending on the way to Portuguese and started to use the word 'mais' instead. The four oldest and most used ones kept their Latin comparative: 'bom' (good) gives 'melhor', 'ruim' or 'mau' (bad) gives 'pior', 'grande' (big) gives 'maior' and 'pequeno' (small) gives 'menor'. English shows the same effect: 'good', 'better' and 'bad', 'worse' are irregular for the same reason, and nobody says 'gooder'. The principle is that these four words already contain the idea of 'more', so adding 'mais' repeats it, like English 'more better'. 'Mais bom' and 'mais melhor' are errors when you mean 'better'.

They behave like other adjectives otherwise. Each has one shape for masculine and feminine and takes '-es' in the plural ('melhores', 'piores', 'maiores', 'menores'), by the same rule that turns 'mulher' into 'mulheres'. To strengthen them, use 'muito' or 'bem' before them: 'muito melhor', 'bem pior'. Never use 'muito mais melhor'.

'Melhor' and 'pior' do a second job. Besides being adjectives that describe nouns, they are also adverbs, words that describe a verb, and they compare the adverbs 'bem' (well) and 'mal' (badly): 'Ela canta melhor do que eu', 'Ele dirige pior do que o irmão'. English does this too with 'better' and 'worse'. 'Mais pequeno' is also heard and correct for size, while 'mais grande' is rare, so 'maior' is the normal choice for 'big'.

Age is regular. 'Velho' (old) and 'novo' (new, young) take 'mais', and they agree with the noun: 'Minha irmã é mais nova do que eu'. The measure phrase goes before 'mais': 'três anos mais velho', literally 'three years more old'. In colloquial Brazilian Portuguese you will also hear 'mais ruim', but 'pior' is the standard choice.

grammar.title: Superlatives: o mais ... de and -íssimo
grammar.explanation:
A superlative says that something has the most or the least of a quality in a whole group. English uses the ending '-est' or the words 'the most' ('the cheapest', 'the most expensive'). Portuguese builds it from the comparative you already know, plus a definite article, the word meaning 'the' ('o', 'a', 'os', 'as'). The logic is that a comparative sets two things against each other, while the article points to one single thing in the group, and the group is named afterwards. The order is article, noun, 'mais' or 'menos', adjective, 'de' and the group: 'Esse é o hotel mais caro da cidade', literally 'the hotel more expensive of-the city'. Where English says 'in the city' or 'in the class', Portuguese says 'of' and fuses it with the article: 'da cidade', 'do Brasil', 'da turma'. The article is the only thing that turns the comparative into a superlative: 'Ela é mais nova' means 'she is younger', and 'Ela é a mais nova' means 'she is the youngest'.

The article agrees with the noun it points to and stands once, directly before the whole phrase: 'o hotel mais caro', 'a cidade mais cara'. If the noun is already known and left out, the article alone stands for it, like the English 'one': 'Qual é o mais barato?' means 'which one is the cheapest?' The irregular comparatives work the same way and usually come before the noun: 'o melhor restaurante da cidade', 'a pior nota da turma', 'a maior cidade do país'.

A separate tool is the suffix '-íssimo'. A suffix is an ending added to a word to change its meaning. Unlike the relative superlative above, it compares with nothing: it just means 'extremely', so it is called the absolute superlative. Drop the final vowel of the adjective and add '-íssimo', which agrees like any adjective in 'o': 'caro', 'caríssimo', 'caríssima', 'caríssimos'. The 'í' always carries an accent because the stress falls on the third to last syllable (ca-RÍS-si-mo), and nothing predicts that. A word has one main stress, so when the base word already had an accent, it goes: 'rápido' becomes 'rapidíssimo' and 'tímido' becomes 'timidíssimo', because the stress moved to the new 'í'. Three spelling changes follow from the sounds. An adjective in '-vel' changes to '-bil-': 'amável' becomes 'amabilíssimo'. A final 'z' becomes 'c', so 'feliz' becomes 'felicíssimo'; the 'c' before 'í' is already the sound [s]. A 'c' or 'g' left at the end of the base becomes 'qu' or 'gu', because 'c' before 'í' would be [s] and 'g' would be [ʒ]: 'rico' becomes 'riquíssimo' and 'largo' becomes 'larguíssimo'. Two everyday adjectives use different words: 'bom' becomes 'ótimo' and 'ruim' becomes 'péssimo'.

Use '-íssimo' for warm, emphatic speech: 'Está caríssimo!' In speech, 'muito', 'super' and 'bem' do the same job with no change of spelling: 'muito caro', 'super legal', 'bem cansado'. In a formal report, prefer 'muito'.

the old accent on 'á' is dropped; the stress moves to the new 'í'

grammar.title: Same, similar, different and preferring
grammar.explanation:
Comparison also says that two things are identical, resemble each other or differ. Each of the three uses an adjective followed by a fixed preposition, where English also uses one: 'the same as', 'similar to', 'different from'. The Portuguese adjective and its preposition are a pair, so learn them together: 'igual a', 'parecido com' and 'diferente de'. An adjective is a word that describes a noun; a preposition is a short word placed before a noun to show how it relates to the rest of the sentence. The adjectives agree with the noun they describe ('iguais', 'parecida', 'diferentes'), and the preposition contracts with a following article where it can: 'igual ao seu' ('a' + 'o'), 'diferente da sua' ('de' + 'a'). 'Com' does not contract: 'parecido com o pai'. 'Igual' becomes 'iguais' in the plural because the final 'l' turns into 'i', the same rule as 'animal' and 'animais'.

'Parecido' comes from the verb 'parecer', to seem, so 'parecido com' is literally 'seemed with'. The verb forms are common on their own: 'Ela parece simpática' means 'she seems friendly', and 'parece que' means 'it seems that'. 'Diferente de' is literally 'different of'. In speech 'igual' also works as a preposition meaning 'like': 'Ela fala igual à mãe'. 'Mais ou menos' is literally 'more or less' and is the all-purpose answer for 'so-so', or for 'roughly' when used with a number.

Pronouns after these prepositions take the prepositional form, not the subject form: 'diferente de mim', 'igual a você'. This is the same contrast as in the comparison note. After 'que' the pronoun completes a short sentence and is 'eu'; after a preposition the form is 'mim'. 'Mim' cannot be used as a subject.

For preferences, Portuguese says 'preferir A a B', literally 'prefer A to B', and English uses the same structure: 'Prefiro café a chá', 'Prefiro o litoral ao interior' ('a' + 'o' = 'ao'). In everyday Brazilian speech you will constantly hear 'preferir A do que B', borrowed from the comparative. Some grammar books dislike it, because 'preferir' already means 'to like more', so adding 'do que' repeats the comparison. The neutral alternative is 'gostar mais de A do que de B'. Opinions are introduced with 'Na minha opinião', literally 'in-the my opinion', or 'Acho que', literally 'I-find that'.

To ask whether something justifies its cost or effort, use 'vale a pena', literally 'is-worth the pain'. 'Pena' is an older word for trouble or effort, so the idea is that the effort pays off. Only 'valer' changes: 'vale a pena', 'valeu a pena', 'não vale a pena'. An infinitive follows it directly: 'Vale a pena esperar'.

grammar.title: Small words and constructions in the dialogues
grammar.explanation:
A few short expressions in the dialogues do not mean what their words say, and a few constructions have not been taught yet. The table gives the literal meaning of each, and this note explains the logic.

'Ficar' is literally 'to stay', and you have met it meaning 'to be located' ('onde fica o banco?'). The same idea gives the meaning 'to become' or 'to get': when something changes and the new state stays, Portuguese says it stayed. 'O Rio pode ficar mais frio' means 'Rio can get colder', and 'fiquei felicíssima' means 'I became extremely happy'. The past form 'fiquei' (I stayed, I became) writes 'qu' instead of 'c' to keep the sound [k] before the ending. 'Achar' is literally 'to find'. 'Acho o preço alto' means 'I find the price high', that is, I think it is high; the adjective describes the thing just named. 'Levar' is 'to carry', so 'eu levo o Alfa' is 'I take it with me', which is how a buyer says 'I will take it'.

'Nossa' is short for 'Nossa Senhora', literally 'Our Lady', and today it is only an exclamation of surprise, like 'wow'. 'Hum' is a hesitating sound, like 'hmm'. 'Fechado', literally 'closed', means 'deal', as in a closed agreement. 'É mesmo' is literally 'it is same', and 'mesmo' means 'really' or 'indeed'; before a noun, 'mesmo' means 'same', as in 'o mesmo time'. 'Torcer' is literally 'to twist'; one popular explanation is that early soccer fans twisted their handkerchiefs while watching. 'Torcer por' means to support a team, and 'por' + 'o' fuses to 'pelo'. 'Todo mundo' is literally 'all world', and means 'everybody'. 'Lá em casa' is 'there in house' and means 'over at my place'; the 'lá' only adds a casual distance. 'A menos', literally 'at less', states a difference: 'trezentos reais a menos' means 'less by three hundred reais'. 'Até' is literally 'until', and also means 'even', as in 'Até o meu pai', even my father.

'Custa', 'dura' and 'ganha' are present tense forms of 'custar' (to cost), 'durar' (to last) and 'ganhar' (to win or to earn). They are regular, so the ending 'a' is the form for 'ele', 'ela' and 'você'.

culture.title: Cities with personality
culture.text:
Brazilians love to compare their cities, and the rivalry is mostly friendly. People from São Paulo, the paulistanos, like to say that their city is the biggest, the busiest and the best for work, while cariocas, from Rio de Janeiro, answer that Rio is the most beautiful and the most relaxed. Someone from Salvador, a soteropolitano, will tell you that the food and the music of Bahia beat both. Mineiros, from Minas Gerais, are known for a quieter, more hospitable way of life and for pão de queijo.

The five official regions of Brazil, the Norte, Nordeste, Centro-Oeste, Sudeste and Sul, differ in climate, accent, food and even vocabulary. The Sul can be cold enough for frost in winter, while much of the Nordeste is warm all year. When you ask locals for an opinion, expect a strong one: 'Essa praia é a melhor do Brasil' is a very normal thing to hear. Learners can join in with safe phrases such as 'na minha opinião' and 'mais ou menos', and with the friendly exaggeration of '-íssimo', as in 'Está caríssimo!'

exercises.prompt_target: Ela é a mais nova ___ três irmãs.
exercises.hint_source: She is the youngest of the three sisters.
exercises.explanation: The group of a superlative is introduced with 'de', which fuses with the article 'as' ('de' + 'as' = 'das').

exercises.prompt_target: Meu quarto é o ___ da casa.
exercises.hint_source: My room is the smallest in the house.
exercises.explanation: 'O menor' is the superlative of 'pequeno', built on the comparative 'menor' plus the article.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'rápido' lose its accent in 'rapidíssimo'?
choices: The accent only appears on adjectives ending in 'o'
Because '-íssimo' always removes the first accent of any word
The stress moves to the new 'í', so the old 'á' is no longer the stressed syllable
exercises.explanation: A word has one main stress. The accent marks the stressed vowel, so it follows the stress to the 'í' of '-íssimo'.

exercises.prompt_target: O hotel é ___. Custa uma fortuna.
exercises.hint_source: The hotel is extremely expensive. It costs a fortune.
exercises.explanation: 'Caro' loses its 'o' and takes '-íssimo'; the 'í' carries the accent because the stress is on the third to last syllable.

exercises.prompt_target: Meu irmão tem vinte anos e eu tenho dezoito. Ele é mais ___ do que eu.
exercises.hint_source: My brother is older than me.
exercises.explanation: Age is regular: 'velho' and 'novo' take 'mais'.

exercises.hint_source: My neighborhood is different from yours.
exercises.explanation: 'Diferente de' takes a following article into the contraction: 'de' + 'o' = 'do'.

exercises.prompt: 'Vale a pena' is literally 'is-worth the pain'. What does it mean?
choices: It hurts
It is worth it
What a pity
exercises.explanation: 'Pena' here is an older word for trouble or effort, so the phrase says the effort pays off.

exercises.prompt: 'Nossa' is short for 'Nossa Senhora', literally 'Our Lady'. What does it mean in everyday speech?
choices: Thank you
Excuse me
Wow
exercises.explanation: It lost its religious sense and is now just an exclamation of surprise.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks 'Como foi o filme?' and you answer 'Mais ou menos.' What do you mean?
choices: It was so-so.
It was great.
It was terrible.
exercises.explanation: 'Mais ou menos' is literally 'more or less', and it is the usual way to say 'so-so'.

exercises.prompt: Match each adjective with its '-íssimo' form
exercises.explanation: Drop the final vowel and add '-íssimo'. 'Rápido' loses its old accent, and 'feliz' changes 'z' to 'c'.

exercises.audio_target: Essa marca é muito melhor, mas é caríssima.
choices: This brand is much worse, but it is very cheap.
This brand is much better, but it is very expensive.
This brand is much better, but it is very slow.

exercises.audio_target: Meu irmão mais novo é igual ao meu pai.
choices: My older brother is just like my father.
My younger brother is different from my father.
My younger brother is just like my father.

exercises.prompt_source: This hotel is cheaper than that one.
She is as tall as her brother.
He is the oldest in the family.
It was the worst trip of my life.
This sofa is as comfortable as my bed.
answers: Este sofá é tão confortável quanto a minha cama.
Este sofá é tão confortável quanto minha cama.
Este sofá é tão confortável como a minha cama.
Esse sofá é tão confortável quanto a minha cama.
Esse sofá é tão confortável quanto minha cama.
Esse sofá é tão confortável como a minha cama.

exercises.prompt_source: My brother is older than me.
answers: Meu irmão é mais velho do que eu.
Meu irmão é mais velho que eu.
O meu irmão é mais velho do que eu.
O meu irmão é mais velho que eu.
exercises.explanation: After 'que' the pronoun is 'eu', because it is the subject of an understood verb.

exercises.prompt_source: I prefer the coast to the countryside.
answers: Eu prefiro o litoral ao interior.
Eu prefiro o litoral do que o interior.
Prefiro o litoral do que o interior.
exercises.explanation: The standard pattern is 'preferir A a B', and 'a' + 'o' contracts to 'ao'. 'Preferir A do que B' is common in speech.

exercises.prompt_source: Who is the youngest in your family?
answers: Quem é o mais novo da sua família?
Quem é a mais nova da sua família?
Quem é o mais novo na sua família?
Quem é a mais nova na sua família?

exercises.audio_target: São Paulo é a maior cidade do Brasil.
exercises.hint_source: São Paulo is the biggest city in Brazil.

exercises.audio_target: Esse celular é tão bom quanto o meu.
exercises.hint_source: This phone is as good as mine.
